reasoning_note: Normally I would dismiss outbound FTP as a legacy job, but the MVE telling me this is a BD Alaris pump that has never used FTP in 120 days with active infusions changes my calculus entirely.
Day-shift billing user hitting 47 cardiology records at 11pm with zero precedent in 90 days is hard to explain away even for a skeptic like me.
Knowing the source is not one of the two authorized biomed workstations removes my usual benefit-of-the-doubt — unauthorized cross-VLAN SMB to medical devices gets blocked.
LIS has never used SFTP in 180 days and the destination is unapproved — I still want to check with Lab IT first but I would block port 22 outbound on that box while I ask.
Destination resolves to a legit Baxter update domain, confidence is low, device is operational — this is exactly the kind of alert I expect to dismiss.
20x DNS volume from a patient monitor could be a firmware check loop but the MVE correctly notes it could also be a beacon, so I will rate-limit and verify with biomed rather than ignore it.
Float pool nurse covering multiple wards on night shift — the MVE confirms this is expected behavior and the access volume is normal.
New asset with no baseline doing an ICMP sweep across all VLANs — I would normally dismiss this as SolarWinds or similar, but since it is a brand new device I should verify with IT ops first.
Saturday biomed maintenance is a real thing that happens quarterly, and the MVE confirms this pattern, so I will just verify with the biomed schedule.
Approved destination, approved partner, volume consistent with a full CT series — the MVE confirms this is a routine second-opinion workflow.
Unlike A-14, this PACS transfer goes to an unapproved destination at 4am — the MVE pointing out embedded PHI in DICOM headers makes this worth blocking and investigating.
An insulin pump getting an unauthorized pairing attempt matching a known wireless vulnerability is the one alert where I drop all skepticism and call the floor immediately.
312 records in 8 minutes from a service account 5 hours before its scheduled run with no precedent in 180 days — even I cannot hand-wave this as a cron job misfire.
Telnet from a ventilator with zero precedent in 365 days on a life-sustaining device — the MVE is right to say block the port but keep the device running.
Internal backup to an approved server, just running at an odd time — almost certainly a rescheduled failed backup, verify with ops and move on.
Approved AWS destination, pharmacy admin system not connected to dispensing, weekend backup timing is slightly off but benign.
Quarterly diagnostic pattern matching a previous baseline event three months ago — textbook false positive, add a suppression rule.
The EHR server port-scanning the entire internal network including clinical device VLANs at 3am is active compromise — even my most skeptical instincts cannot explain this away.
Physician accessing his own patient panel via authorized VPN at 9:45pm is the most normal thing in this entire alert set.
1.1 GB in 3 minutes from a nurse station that never initiates external traffic at a velocity exceeding human capability — the MVE is right, this is automated exfiltration, isolate now.

q21_note: The MVE sections explicitly name device types, patient counts, wards, and care disruption risks in language a clinician can act on without needing to understand network protocols.
q22_note: Each alert includes baseline behavior, confidence levels, specific recommended actions with safeguards, and escalation paths that give management everything they need to approve or challenge my call.
